Stopping Power vs. Depth

Total stopping power along the beam path through all layers

Method: for each layer the input CSDA range R(Ein) is read off the tabulated curve for that layer's material, the layer's mass thickness Δx (thickness × density, or entered directly in g/cm²) is subtracted to give the residual range R(Ein)−Δx, and this is inverted back through the same monotonic R(E) curve (log–log interpolation, no extrapolation) to obtain the residual energy — the exact tabulated-data analogue of the Bragg Peak tab's range-subtraction method, rather than a thin-layer S(E)·Δx approximation. (The rendered depth plot below Rmin uses the same low-energy/end-of-range phenomenological taper as the Bragg Peak tab — Theory §11 — which is extrapolated, not tabulated.) If a layer's mass thickness exceeds the remaining CSDA range the beam is reported as fully stopped in that layer, and the depth plot shows the stopping power falling to zero at that point (dashed red boundary in the diagram). Valid for particles that travel in near-straight lines (protons, alphas); for electrons, large-angle multiple Coulomb scattering means the true penetration depth can be markedly less than the path length this calculation tracks.

Statistically optimized universal low-energy model

Universal low-energy stopping-power formula

A single closed-form model for the low-energy branch, valid for any projectile mass $M$ and any material $(I,\,Z/A)$ — no per-material fitting. The global coefficients are obtained by minimizing the aggregate relative-residual objective across the embedded PSTAR/ASTAR systems, with AIC/BIC used to judge the added low-energy correction.

Below, the Coefficient source control switches between the boxed global numbers (identical for all 148 systems, shown below) and a per-material fit that re-optimizes the coefficients using only the selected material's own NIST points. Because a single material fixes $M$, $I$, and $Z/A$, the four-term power laws for $C_m$ and $E_t$ can't be separated from a single prefactor with one material's data — so the per-material fit directly optimizes 8 effective numbers ($C_m$, $E_t$, $q$, $a$, $A_p$, $\lambda_p$, $\sigma_L$, $\sigma_R$) for that material, run client-side with a Nelder–Mead simplex search, rather than re-deriving separate $M/I/(Z/A)$ exponents.
$$S_{\rm base}(E)=\big[1-F(\xi)\big]\,C_m\sqrt{E}\,G(\xi)+F(\xi)S_{\rm BB}(E),\qquad \xi=E/E_t,\qquad F(\xi)=1-e^{-\xi^{q}}$$ $$G(\xi)=\exp\!\left[a\frac{\sqrt{\xi}}{1+\sqrt{\xi}}\right]$$ $$\boxed{S_e(E)=S_{\rm base}(E)\left[1+A_pP(E)\right]}$$ $$E_p=\lambda_pE_t,\qquad P(E)=\begin{cases}\exp\!\left[-\dfrac{\ln^2(E/E_p)}{2\sigma_L^2}\right],&E\lt E_p\\[4pt]\exp\!\left[-\dfrac{\ln^2(E/E_p)}{2\sigma_R^2}\right],&E\ge E_p\end{cases}$$ $$\boxed{C_m=2.28102\times10^{5}M^{-0.09008}\left(\dfrac{I}{1\,\rm eV}\right)^{-0.70954}\left(\dfrac{Z}{A}\right)^{0.62120}}$$ $$\boxed{E_t=2.74830\times10^{-6}M^{1.57799}\left(\dfrac{I}{1\,\rm eV}\right)^{0.24764}\left(\dfrac{Z}{A}\right)^{0.48478}\ {\rm MeV}}$$ $$\boxed{q=1.68961,\qquad a=1.18646}$$ $$\boxed{A_p=-0.71065,\qquad \lambda_p=1.05692,\qquad \sigma_L=1.50633,\qquad \sigma_R=0.64294}$$

The coefficients were re-optimized 2026-09-01 by a single joint least-squares fit of all 14 parameters above against all 18,870 tabulated points across the embedded 148 PSTAR/ASTAR systems, reducing aggregate χ² (5% reference tolerance) from 333,935 to 84,063 (reduced χ² 17.70→4.46, MAPE 12.88%→6.07%). Two signs flipped relative to the previous fit: $a$ is now positive and $A_p$ is now negative — jointly, a smoother transition ($q$ dropped from 5.84 to 1.69) paired with a localized *dip* rather than a boost near $E_p$ fits the aggregate data better. The extra factor $G(\xi)$ is a bounded low-energy curvature correction: it tends to 1 as $E\to0$ and remains positive regardless of the sign of $a$, so it cannot create an unphysical negative stopping power. The asymmetric log-energy peak factor is localized around $E_p=\lambda_pE_t$ and tends to 1 far from the transition, so it corrects the localized model/NIST mismatch near the transition without changing the asymptotic low- or high-energy limits. Model selection is reported with a 5% relative reference tolerance; this is a model-discrepancy diagnostic, not an asserted point-by-point NIST uncertainty.

TermBasisWhy it's in the formula
$[1-F(\xi)]\,C_m\sqrt E + F(\xi)\,S_{\rm BB}$ blendStructuralNIST electronic stopping power is only ever one physical curve, but no single closed form covers both ends: Bethe–Bloch is a high-velocity Born-approximation expansion in $\ln(\cdot)/\beta^2$ that diverges/breaks down as $\beta\to0$, while the deep sub-keV data follows a simple near-$\sqrt E$ trend. A smooth interpolation between two valid asymptotic forms is the standard way to bridge a regime a single perturbative expansion can't reach — nothing here is fitted "just because," each branch is separately motivated below.
$C_m\sqrt E$ (low-energy branch)Empirical, but physically motivatedLindhard–Scharff theory predicts electronic stopping $\propto v \propto \sqrt E$ for a slow, partially-screened ion below the electron Fermi velocity — this is the textbook low-velocity limit, not an arbitrary power law. $C_m$ was left as a free coefficient per system and fit to the first five NIST points (1–3 keV) specifically because those points sit deepest in the regime where Lindhard–Scharff applies and Bethe–Bloch is least trustworthy.
$S_{\rm BB}(E)$ (high-energy branch)Physical (Bethe–Bloch + standard corrections)Above roughly $E_t$, electronic stopping is well described by the first-Born Bethe–Bloch formula once density-effect, shell, Barkas, Bloch and effective-charge terms are added — this is the same corrected model already validated against NIST elsewhere in this app, reused here rather than re-derived.
$F(\xi)=1-e^{-\xi^{q}}$, $\xi=E/E_t$Structural choice, not derivedAny monotonic function going 0→1 as $E$ crosses $E_t$ would blend the branches; this particular smooth-step form was chosen because it is $C^\infty$ (no kink at the crossover, unlike a hard switch or piecewise-linear ramp), asymptotes cleanly to each branch far from $E_t$, and needs only one shape parameter ($q$) beyond the crossover scale itself. $E_t$ was then defined as *where the two branches cross*, i.e. fit directly against the NIST transition region — that is what makes $E_t$ a physically meaningful quantity worth scaling with $M,I,Z/A$ rather than an arbitrary knob.
$q=1.68961$Jointly re-optimized (2026-09-01)$q$ sets how abruptly the transition happens — larger $q$ means a sharper step, smaller $q$ a more gradual blend. It is fit jointly with all 13 other parameters against the full 18,870-point table, so $E_t$'s reported value is only meaningful together with this $q$; changing $q$ without re-fitting the rest shifts the effective crossover. The slider in this tab lets you see that sensitivity directly, and 1.68961 is the value the formulas above were actually calibrated against.
$C_m,E_t \propto I^{a}$Empirical (data-driven)The mean excitation energy $I$ is the single number that already governs the high-energy Bethe–Bloch logarithm, so it's the first candidate variable to test for the low-energy coefficients too. Power-law exponents in $I$ ($a\approx-0.71$ for $C_m$, $+0.25$ for $E_t$) were fit directly against the 148-system table rather than derived from first principles — they are what a joint regression against real NIST data actually needed to collapse the scatter.
$C_m,E_t \propto (Z/A)^{b}$Empirical (data-driven)$Z/A$ sets the target electron density per unit mass, which is the other quantity multiplying every Bethe-type stopping formula. It was tested as a second scaling variable once $I$ alone left residual material-to-material scatter, and included because it measurably improved the collapse ($b\approx0.62$ for $C_m$, $+0.48$ for $E_t$) — not assumed a priori.
$C_m,E_t \propto M^{p}$Empirical, deliberately not forced to a theory valueAdded specifically to unify the separate proton and alpha formulas into one $M$-explicit expression. A pure velocity-threshold argument ($E\propto\tfrac12 Mv^2$ at fixed $v_t$) predicts $p=1$ for $E_t$; the joint 14-parameter regression instead gives $p\approx1.58$ for $E_t$ (and a small, near-flat $p\approx-0.09$ for $C_m$), reported here as a real empirical result rather than being rounded to the theoretically "nicer" value of 1 — see the note above the table.
$C_m\sqrt{E}\,G(\xi)$ — Corrected low-energy branchPlotted trace (dashed cyan)The Lindhard–Scharff term alone, multiplied by the curvature factor $G(\xi)$, plotted on its own with no blend against $S_{\rm BB}$ and no peak correction applied. It shows how far the low-energy asymptote would extrapolate by itself, and is the same quantity the table above calls correctedSlow.
$S_{\rm base}(E)=[1-F(\xi)]\,C_m\sqrt{E}\,G(\xi)+F(\xi)\,S_{\rm BB}(E)$ — Base universal modelPlotted trace (dotted gray)The corrected low-energy branch above, smoothly blended into the Bethe–Bloch branch $S_{\rm BB}(E)$ by the transition function $F(\xi)$ — this is the model before the localized peak correction is applied, i.e. base in the code.
$S_e(E)=S_{\rm base}(E)\big[1+A_pP(E)\big]$ — Universal model + peak correctionPlotted trace (solid purple)The base model above multiplied by the localized asymmetric log-Gaussian peak factor $P(E)$ (centered at $E_p=\lambda_pE_t$, width $\sigma_L$ below and $\sigma_R$ above). This is the final boxed formula, total in the code, and is the curve actually compared to NIST for χ², MAPE, and RMS% in the stats row below the plot.

Reduced-complexity model selection

Low-energy law comparison: Models 1 → 2 → 3

Three progressively richer low-energy laws, each blended into the same fixed corrected Bethe–Bloch high-energy branch, are fit independently to the selected NIST system to test how much complexity the data supports. Model 1 uses the baseline $C\sqrt{E}$ law, Model 2 adds the crossover scale $E_t$, and Model 3 uses the generalized power law $C E^n$ together with $E_t$ and $a$. The generalized Model 3 already provides the required free power exponent $n$ for both PSTAR and ASTAR. No peak correction is applied here — this isolates the low-energy law itself.

$$\boxed{\text{Model 1 (1 parameter): } S_{\rm low}^{(1)}(E)=C\sqrt{E}}$$
Free parameter: $C$
$$\boxed{\text{Model 2 (2 parameters): } S_{\rm low}^{(2)}(E)=C\sqrt{E}\,\exp\!\left[\frac{1}{1+E/E_t}\right]}$$
Free parameters: $C,\ E_t$
$$\boxed{\text{Model 3 (4 parameters): } S_{\rm low}^{(3)}(E)=C E^n\,\exp\!\left[\frac{a}{1+E/E_t}\right]}$$
Free parameters: $C,\ E_t,\ a,\ n$
$$S^{(k)}(E)=\big[1-F(\xi)\big]\,S_{\rm low}^{(k)}(E)+F(\xi)\,S_{\rm BB}(E),\qquad \xi=E/E_t,\qquad F(\xi)=1-e^{-\xi^{q}}$$

All three share the same fixed global crossover exponent $q=1.68961$ and the same full corrected Bethe–Bloch branch $S_{\rm BB}(E)$ (Theory §2) — only the low-energy parameters listed above are fitted, per material, by Nelder–Mead against the log-residual objective. Model 1 uses the global scaling-law $E_t$ (Universal Model tab); Models 2–3 fit $E_t$ directly; Model 3 also fits the power exponent $n$.

Global Reduced-Parameter Scaling Fit

Joint fit of C, E_t, a and n across all PSTAR + ASTAR materials
Not calculated

Instead of fitting C, E_t and a independently for every material, this fit constrains them to global material-scaling laws. The candidate models use 4, 8 and 13 free coefficients respectively; Model 3 adds the global power exponent n. The crossover exponent q = 1.68961 and the corrected Bethe–Bloch branch remain fixed.

Scaling laws:
$$C=C_0\left(\frac{M}{M_p}\right)^{c_M}\left(\frac{I}{100\,\mathrm{eV}}\right)^{c_I}\left(\frac{Z/A}{0.5}\right)^{c_Z}$$ $$E_t=E_0\left(\frac{M}{M_p}\right)^{t_M}\left(\frac{I}{100\,\mathrm{eV}}\right)^{t_I}\left(\frac{Z/A}{0.5}\right)^{t_Z}$$ $$a=a_0+a_M\ln\left(\frac{M}{M_p}\right)+a_I\ln\left(\frac{I}{100\,\mathrm{eV}}\right)+a_Z\ln\left(\frac{Z/A}{0.5}\right),\qquad n=n_0$$
Model 1 fits only C (4 parameters); Model 2 fits C and E_t (8); Model 3 fits C, E_t, a and a global n (13).

Units: MeV·cm²/g. Electron-only view of the Comparison tab. Møller is the bare Møller/Berger–Seltzer collision formula with no corrections. BB adds the shell, Barkas and Bloch corrections (evaluated at electron kinematics) but leaves the density effect off. BB + density (compact) switches on the original asymptote-only density-effect term δ used elsewhere in this app. BB + density (Sternheimer) uses the same shell/Barkas/Bloch corrections but replaces δ with the full Sternheimer-Peierls bridge (§2.1). BB + density (DRDM) uses a new smooth dielectric-response onset derived from I and plasma energy Ep; it is a zero-free-parameter candidate that preserves the compact high-energy asymptote. All three density variants are plotted for direct validation against NIST. NIST ESTAR collision stopping power is the reference data. Effective charge does not apply to electrons, so it is not part of this cascade.

Precision note on δ: the chart now plots two density-effect variants of BB+density, both evaluated at the electron's own β,γ: a compact plasma-frequency asymptote (hard-clamped at δ=0), and a Sternheimer-Peierls model that reconstructs the full three-branch δ(X) curve — including the smooth $X_0\to X_1$ bridge the compact model skips — using universal (non-conductor) $X_0,X_1,m$ rules and an $a$ fixed by continuity at $X_0$, so it needs no extra per-material Sternheimer table. The two agree exactly above $X_1$; they diverge in the intermediate-energy region, which is exactly where the compact model's hard clamp is least accurate. Precision NIST calculations instead use individually tabulated $C,a,m,X_0,X_1$ per material — see Theory → §2 for detail — so even the Sternheimer-Peierls curve here remains a physics-based approximation to, not a byte-for-byte reproduction of, the NIST correction. DRDM is additionally shown as a zero-free-parameter dielectric-response onset model: it uses the atomic scale I and collective plasma scale Ep=28.816√(ρZ/A) eV to replace the compact hard clamp by a smooth softplus crossover while preserving the same high-energy asymptote.

Depth–dose curve
Relative dose vs. depth
Relative doseBragg peakR90 / R80 / R50 (distal)
LandmarkDepthResidual rangeResidual energy (MeV)Relative dose

Model: at each depth $x$ the residual CSDA range is $R(x)=R_{\text{CSDA}}(E_0)-x$; the residual energy $E(x)$ is found by inverting the tabulated $R_{\text{CSDA}}(E)$ curve, and relative dose is taken proportional to the total mass stopping power $S(E(x))$, normalized to its maximum. Because the stopping-power maximum sits extremely close to the end of range (for 150 MeV protons in water it occupies roughly the last 0.001% of the ~16 g/cm² path), the depth grid is sampled log-spaced in residual range rather than linear in depth, so resolution automatically concentrates where the curve is sharp. R90/R80/R50 are the distal depths (beyond the peak) where dose falls to 90%/80%/50% of the peak. Multiple Coulomb scattering, range straggling, and nuclear-interaction buildup/falloff are not modeled, so this idealized CSDA curve peaks far more sharply — and with a far higher peak-to-entrance ratio — than a real measured Bragg curve, which straggling broadens substantially. Electrons do not exhibit a true Bragg peak.

Physics reference

Stopping-Power, Universal-Model & Range Theory

This section documents the equations actually used by the application: Bethe–Bloch and its correction layers, electron Møller/Berger–Seltzer stopping, density-effect variants, radiative and nuclear stopping, compound rules, effective material quantities, interpolation, CSDA range, Bragg-curve construction, multilayer attenuation, the Universal Model, reduced models, fitting statistics, and the CBB $Z_{\rm eff}$ inversion.

1 · Definitions 2 · Bethe–Bloch 3 · Corrections 4 · Electron collision 5 · Radiative 6 · Nuclear 7 · Mixtures 8 · $Z_{\rm eff}$/$A_{\rm eff}$ 9 · CSDA range 10 · Interpolation 11 · Bragg curve 12 · Multilayer attenuation 13 · Universal Model 14 · Reduced Models 15 · CBB $Z_{\rm eff}$ fit 16 · Statistics 17 · Proton/alpha scaling Symbols Limitations

1 · Stopping-power definitions and particle branches

The application works with mass stopping power, so the material density is divided out. The Calculator then reconstructs linear stopping power when needed.

EquationUsed for
$$S(E)\equiv-\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dE}{dx}$$Mass stopping power, in MeV·cm²/g.
$$-\frac{dE}{dx}=\rho\,S(E)$$Linear stopping power, in MeV/cm.
$$S_{\rm total}=S_{\rm col}+S_{\rm rad}$$ESTAR electron total stopping power.
$$S_{\rm total}=S_{\rm elec}+S_{\rm nuc}$$PSTAR/ASTAR total stopping power.

Relativistic kinematics used by the heavy-particle branch

EquationMeaning
$$\gamma=1+\frac{E}{Mc^2}$$Relativistic factor from kinetic energy.
$$\beta^2=1-\frac{1}{\gamma^2},\qquad \beta=\frac{v}{c}$$Projectile speed in units of $c$.
$$\beta\gamma=\sqrt{\gamma^2-1}$$Convenient density/shell-correction variable.

Important implementation distinction: protons and alpha particles use the corrected Bethe–Bloch branch; electrons use the separate Møller/Berger–Seltzer collision branch. The ESTAR radiative term is not reconstructed from the electron collision formula.

2 · Bethe–Bloch backbone for protons and alpha particles

The code evaluates a transparent corrected Bethe–Bloch model for PSTAR/ASTAR comparisons. The leading stopping number is formed first, then density, shell, Barkas and Bloch corrections are inserted, while the projectile effective charge modifies the overall $z^2$ strength.

Equation used in calculationRole
$$S_{\rm BB}=K\frac{Z}{A}\frac{z^2}{\beta^2}L_0$$Uncorrected Bethe–Bloch stopping power.
$$L_0=\frac12\ln\!\left(\frac{2m_ec^2\beta^2\gamma^2T_{\max}}{I^2}\right)-\beta^2$$Base stopping number.
$$T_{\max}=\frac{2m_ec^2\beta^2\gamma^2}{1+2\gamma m_e/M+(m_e/M)^2}$$Maximum kinetic energy transferable to a target electron.
$$S_{\rm corr}=K\frac{Z}{A}\frac{z^2}{\beta^2}z_q\!\left[L_0-\frac{\delta}{2}-\frac{C}{Z_{\rm eff}}+zB_{\rm Barkas}+z^2B_{\rm Bloch}\right]$$Full corrected model implemented for heavy particles.

Code detail: the denominator of the shell term is the composition-average $Z_{\rm eff}$ for compounds/mixtures. The material's stored $Z/A$ remains the leading electron-density factor.

3 · Correction layers used by the Comparison and Electron tabs

3.1 Density effect

The calculator exposes three density-effect formulations. They share the same collective plasma-energy scale but differ in how the low/intermediate-energy onset is modeled. The density correction enters the stopping-number bracket as $-\delta/2$ for the heavy-particle Bethe–Bloch branch and with the corresponding negative density term in the electron collision branch.

Model / equationDefinition and use in this calculator
Common plasma-energy scale
$$E_p=\hbar\omega_p\,[{\rm eV}]\approx28.816\sqrt{\rho\,Z/A}$$		$E_p$ is the collective plasma-energy scale used by all three models. Here $\rho$ is in g/cm$^3$ and $Z/A$ is the material electron-density factor.
1. Compact density effect
$$\boxed{\delta_{\rm compact}=\max\!\left[0,\;2\ln\!\left(\frac{E_p}{I_{\rm eV}}\right)+2\ln(\beta\gamma)-1\right]}$$
Equivalent form:
$$\delta_{\rm compact}=\max\left[0,\;4.6052X+C_\delta\right]$$
$$X=\log_{10}(\beta\gamma),\qquad C_\delta=2\ln(E_p/I_{\rm eV})-1$$		Asymptote-only model. It uses the high-energy Sternheimer asymptote and applies a hard $\delta=0$ clamp. It is simple and is retained as the original compact option in the calculator, but it does not contain the intermediate-energy Sternheimer bridge.
2. Sternheimer–Peierls density effect
$$\boxed{\delta_{\rm SP}(X)=\begin{cases}0,&X\lt X_0\\4.6052X+C_\delta+a(X_1-X)^m,&X_0\le X\lt X_1\\4.6052X+C_\delta,&X\ge X_1\end{cases}}$$
$$X=\log_{10}(\beta\gamma),\qquad C_\delta=2\ln(E_p/I_{\rm eV})-1$$
$$X_0=0.2,\quad X_1=\begin{cases}2,&I\lt 100\,{\rm\,eV}\\3,&I\ge100\,{\rm\,eV}\end{cases},\quad m=3$$
$$a=-\frac{4.6052X_0+C_\delta}{(X_1-X_0)^m}$$		Three-branch model. It has a low-$X$ region with no density effect, a cubic intermediate-energy bridge, and the same high-energy asymptote as the compact model. In this calculator, universal non-conductor values are used when material-specific Sternheimer coefficients are unavailable.
3. DRDM-P (Dielectric-Response Density Model)
$$E_p=28.816\sqrt{\rho Z/A},\qquad C_\delta=2\ln(E_p/I_{\rm eV})-1$$
$$X=\log_{10}(\beta\gamma)$$
$$X_0=A_0+A_1\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{I_{\rm eV}}{E_p}\right)$$
$$X_1=X_0+\Delta X$$
$$A_0=0.26,\quad A_1=0.21,\quad \Delta X=3.05$$
$$a=\frac{-(4.6052X_0+C_\delta)}{(\Delta X)^3}\quad\text{when }4.6052X_0+C_\delta\lt 0$$
$$\boxed{\delta_{\rm DRDM-P}(X)=\begin{cases}0,&X\le X_0\\4.6052X+C_\delta+a(X_1-X)^3,&X_0\lt X\lt X_1\\4.6052X+C_\delta,&X\ge X_1\end{cases}}$$		Zero-free-parameter dielectric-response onset model. It uses the two physical material scales already available in the database, $I$ and $E_p$, to determine the onset $X_0$ and the bridge width. It replaces the compact model's hard clamp with a smooth material-dependent cubic transition while preserving the exact same high-energy asymptote. It is a proposed model in this calculator, not the tabulated NIST/Sternheimer correction.
The important idea. The new model has only three universal shape constants: $$\boxed{(A_0,A_1,\Delta X)=(0.26,\;0.21,\;3.05)}$$ while the material-specific physics comes from $$\boxed{I,\quad \rho,\quad Z/A}$$ rather than introducing a separate fitted density-effect parameter for every material.
Compact vs Sternheimer–Peierls

The compact model keeps only the asymptotic form $4.6052X+C_\delta$ and clamps it to zero. Sternheimer–Peierls adds the physically motivated intermediate $X_0\rightarrow X_1$ bridge. Therefore the two models are identical for $X\ge X_1$ but can differ substantially in the intermediate-energy region.

Sternheimer–Peierls vs DRDM-P

Sternheimer–Peierls uses prescribed universal $X_0$, $X_1$, and $m$ rules in this calculator and reconstructs the traditional three-branch Sternheimer shape. DRDM-P instead derives its onset scale from the material ratio $I/E_p$, using $A_0=0.26$, $A_1=0.21$, and $\Delta X=3.05$. Both share the same high-energy asymptote, but their intermediate-energy bridges are different.

Important distinction from NIST

For precision stopping-power work, NIST uses material-specific Sternheimer parameters. The Sternheimer–Peierls and DRDM-P implementations shown here are therefore model reconstructions/approximations for validation, not claims of reproducing every NIST material coefficient exactly. DRDM-P is additionally a new candidate dielectric-response model.

Side-by-side: Sternheimer–Peierls (2) vs DRDM-P (3), same equation order
Quantity2 · Sternheimer–Peierls3 · DRDM-P
Plasma energy $E_p$$$E_p=28.816\sqrt{\rho\,Z/A}\ \ {\rm eV}\quad\text{(identical in both models)}$$
Offset $C_\delta$$$C_\delta=2\ln(E_p/I_{\rm eV})-1\quad\text{(identical in both models)}$$
Reduced velocity$$X=\log_{10}(\beta\gamma)\quad\text{(identical in both models)}$$
Onset $X_0$$$X_0=0.2\ \ \text{(fixed constant)}$$$$X_0=A_0+A_1\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{I_{\rm eV}}{E_p}\right)\ \ \text{(material-dependent, from }I,E_p\text{)}$$
Bridge end $X_1$$$X_1=\begin{cases}2,&I\lt 100\,{\rm eV}\\3,&I\ge100\,{\rm eV}\end{cases}\ \ \text{(two-valued step rule)}$$$$X_1=X_0+\Delta X,\quad \Delta X=3.05\ \ \text{(continuous, tracks }X_0\text{)}$$
Bridge exponent$$m=3\ \ \text{(fixed)}$$$$\text{cubic exponent }=3\ \ \text{(same power, applied over }X_1-X_0=\Delta X\text{)}$$
Bridge coefficient $a$$$a=-\frac{4.6052X_0+C_\delta}{(X_1-X_0)^m}$$$$a=\frac{-(4.6052X_0+C_\delta)}{(\Delta X)^3}\quad\text{when }4.6052X_0+C_\delta\lt 0$$
Piecewise $\delta(X)$$$\boxed{\delta_{\rm SP}(X)=\begin{cases}0,&X\lt X_0\\4.6052X+C_\delta+a(X_1-X)^m,&X_0\le X\lt X_1\\4.6052X+C_\delta,&X\ge X_1\end{cases}}$$$$\boxed{\delta_{\rm DRDM-P}(X)=\begin{cases}0,&X\le X_0\\4.6052X+C_\delta+a(X_1-X)^3,&X_0\lt X\lt X_1\\4.6052X+C_\delta,&X\ge X_1\end{cases}}$$
Free per-material fit parameters0 numerically tabulated, but $X_0,X_1,m$ are prescribed step-rule constants, not derived from $I,\rho,Z/A$ continuously.0 — $X_0$ and $X_1$ are smooth, closed-form functions of $I,\rho,Z/A$ through $A_0,A_1,\Delta X$ only.

Reading the table row by row: the top three rows ($E_p$, $C_\delta$, $X$) are shared inputs identical between the two models. The difference lives entirely in how $X_0$ and $X_1$ are set — Sternheimer–Peierls uses fixed/step-rule constants, while DRDM-P derives them smoothly from $I,\rho,Z/A$ via the three universal shape constants $(A_0,A_1,\Delta X)$ — after which both models close with the same three-branch piecewise form and the same high-energy asymptote $4.6052X+C_\delta$.

Implementation note: for the Sternheimer branch, the code uses $a>0$ only when $4.6052X_0+C_\delta\lt 0$; otherwise it sets $a=0$. For DRDM-P the same positivity condition is applied to the cubic bridge coefficient. This preserves the implementation's explicit clamp behavior in edge cases.

3.2 Shell correction

EquationUse
$$C_{\rm shell}=\left(\frac{0.422377}{(\beta\gamma)^2}+\frac{0.0304043}{(\beta\gamma)^4}-\frac{0.00038106}{(\beta\gamma)^6}\right)10^{-6}I_{\rm eV}^2+\left(\frac{3.850190}{(\beta\gamma)^2}-\frac{0.1667989}{(\beta\gamma)^4}+\frac{0.00157955}{(\beta\gamma)^6}\right)10^{-9}I_{\rm eV}^3$$Walske/Bichsel-type asymptotic shell correction, evaluated only for $\beta\gamma\ge0.1$.
$$\Delta L_{\rm shell}=-\frac{C_{\rm shell}}{Z_{\rm eff}}$$Insertion into the stopping-number bracket.
$$C_{\rm shell}=0\qquad(\beta\gamma\lt 0.1)$$Explicit implementation cutoff rather than extrapolation beyond the stated validity range.

3.3 Barkas correction

EquationUse
$$y=\frac{z\alpha}{\beta},\qquad \alpha\simeq\frac1{137.036}$$Coulomb parameter.
$$B_{\rm Barkas}\approx\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{z}{137.036\,\beta}$$First-order odd-in-charge Barkas term.
$$\Delta L_{\rm Barkas}=zB_{\rm Barkas}$$Correction inserted into the stopping-number bracket.

3.4 Bloch correction

EquationUse
$$B_{\rm Bloch}=-y^2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n(n^2+y^2)}$$Higher-order Coulomb correction; the code evaluates the convergent series numerically.
$$\Delta L_{\rm Bloch}=z^2B_{\rm Bloch}$$Correction inserted into the stopping-number bracket.

3.5 Effective projectile charge

EquationUse
$$z_{\rm eff}=z\left[1-\exp\!\left(-125\,\frac{\beta}{z^{2/3}}\right)\right]$$Low-velocity charge-state model used for alpha particles.
$$z_q=\left(\frac{z_{\rm eff}}{z}\right)^2$$Multiplicative charge-state factor applied to the overall $z^2$ strength.
$$z_{\rm eff}=1,\quad z_q=1\qquad{\rm (proton)}$$Protons remain fully stripped in this implementation.

3.6 Final correction combination

EquationMeaning
$$\boxed{S_{\rm corr}=K\frac{Z}{A}\frac{z^2}{\beta^2}\left(\frac{z_{\rm eff}}{z}\right)^2\left[L_0-\frac{\delta}{2}-\frac{C_{\rm shell}}{Z_{\rm eff}}+zB_{\rm Barkas}+z^2B_{\rm Bloch}\right]}$$Final corrected PSTAR/ASTAR comparison model.
$$S_{\rm BB}\rightarrow S_{\rm BB+\delta}\rightarrow +{\rm shell}\rightarrow +{\rm Barkas}\rightarrow +{\rm Bloch}\rightarrow +z_{\rm eff}$$Cumulative order shown by the interactive correction curves.

4 · Electron collision stopping power: Møller / Berger–Seltzer branch

For ESTAR, the code does not use the heavy-particle Bethe–Bloch formula as the primary collision equation. It uses the Møller/Berger–Seltzer form appropriate to an electron projectile and an electron target.

EquationUse
$$\tau=\frac{T}{m_ec^2}$$Electron kinetic energy in rest-energy units.
$$\gamma=\tau+1$$Electron Lorentz factor.
$$\beta^2=1-\frac{1}{(\tau+1)^2}$$Electron velocity-squared.
$$F^-(\tau)=1-\beta^2+\frac{\tau^2/8-(2\tau+1)\ln2}{(\tau+1)^2}$$Møller exchange/identical-particle correction.
$$S_{\rm col}^{\rm bare}=\frac{K}{2}\frac{Z}{A}\frac1{\beta^2}\left[\ln\!\frac{\tau^2(\tau+2)}{2(I/m_ec^2)^2}+F^-(\tau)\right]$$Bare Møller collision stopping power — density, shell, Barkas and Bloch all off (used as the uncorrected reference curve).
$$\boxed{S_{\rm col}=\frac{K}{2}\frac{Z}{A}\frac1{\beta^2}\left[\ln\!\frac{\tau^2(\tau+2)}{2(I/m_ec^2)^2}+F^-(\tau)-\delta-\frac{C_{\rm shell}}{Z_{\rm eff}}-B_{\rm Barkas}^{e}+B_{\rm Bloch}\right]}$$Fully corrected electron collision stopping power actually used by the Electron and Comparison tabs by default.
$$y=\frac{\alpha}{\beta},\qquad B_{\rm Barkas}^{e}=\frac\pi2\,y,\qquad B_{\rm Bloch}=-y^2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n(n^2+y^2)}$$Same $C_{\rm shell}$ (§3.2) and Bloch series (§3.4) as the heavy-particle branch, evaluated at $|z|=1$; $B_{\rm Barkas}^e$ enters with a flipped sign relative to the proton/alpha case (see note below).

Electron correction cascade in this app: Møller bare → shell → Barkas (sign flipped, appropriate to a negative projectile) → Bloch (even in charge, same value a proton would have at the same $\beta$) → compact density or Sternheimer density. Shell, Barkas, Bloch and density are each independently toggleable in the Electron/Comparison tabs and are all on by default — the boxed equation above, not the bare one, is what those tabs plot and tabulate unless a correction is explicitly switched off. Effective projectile charge is intentionally inactive for electrons (no bound-electron pickup for a bare lepton).

5 · Electron radiative stopping power

EquationUse / implementation status
$$S_{\rm rad}\approx\frac{N_A}{A}E\,\sigma_{\rm rad}(Z,E)$$Physical relation used to describe radiative loss.
$$S_{\rm total}=S_{\rm col}+S_{\rm rad}$$ESTAR total stopping power.
$$E_c\approx\frac{610}{Z+1.24}\ {\rm MeV}$$Useful solid-material estimate for the collision/radiative crossover.
$$f_{\rm rad}=\frac{S_{\rm rad}}{S_{\rm col}+S_{\rm rad}}$$Radiative fraction displayed by the Calculator.

The code does not reconstruct $\sigma_{\rm rad}$ analytically over the full energy range. The supplied ESTAR radiative column is therefore treated as the reference data; the analytic electron comparison concerns collision stopping power.

6 · Nuclear stopping power for protons and alpha particles

EquationUse
$$S_{\rm nuc}=\frac{N_A}{A}\int T\,\frac{d\sigma}{dT}\,dT$$Energy transferred to target nuclei through screened elastic Coulomb scattering.
$$S_{\rm total}=S_{\rm elec}+S_{\rm nuc}$$Total PSTAR/ASTAR stopping power.
$$f_{\rm elec}=\frac{S_{\rm elec}}{S_{\rm elec}+S_{\rm nuc}},\qquad f_{\rm nuc}=\frac{S_{\rm nuc}}{S_{\rm elec}+S_{\rm nuc}}$$Fractions shown in the material panel.

The application does not evaluate a closed ZBL differential cross-section inside the browser from first principles; the nuclear stopping values come from the supplied PSTAR/ASTAR data.

7 · Compounds and mixtures

EquationUse
$$S_{\rm compound}\approx\sum_iw_iS_i$$Bragg additivity for the leading electronic stopping contribution.
$$\left(\frac ZA\right)_{\rm mix}=\sum_iw_i\frac{Z_i}{A_i}$$Composition-weighted stopping-power electron-density factor.
$$n_e=\rho N_A\sum_iw_i\frac{Z_i}{A_i}=\rho N_A\left(\frac ZA\right)_{\rm mix}$$Electron number density.
$$\ln I_{\rm mix}=\frac{\sum_iw_i(Z_i/A_i)\ln I_i}{\sum_iw_i(Z_i/A_i)}$$Documented log-weighted mixture rule for mean excitation energy metadata.

8 · Composition-average $Z_{\rm eff}$ and $A_{\rm eff}$

These quantities are composition averages used by the application. They are not a universal photon-interaction effective atomic number.

EquationUse
$$f_i=\frac{w_i/A_i}{\sum_jw_j/A_j},\qquad\sum_if_i=1$$Convert mass fractions to atomic fractions.
$$A_{\rm eff}=\sum_if_iA_i=\frac1{\sum_iw_i/A_i}$$Atom-fraction-weighted effective mass.
$$Z_{\rm eff}=\sum_if_iZ_i=\frac{\sum_iw_iZ_i/A_i}{\sum_iw_i/A_i}$$Atom-fraction-weighted effective atomic number.
$$\frac{Z_{\rm eff}}{A_{\rm eff}}=\sum_iw_i\frac{Z_i}{A_i}=\left(\frac ZA\right)_{\rm mix}$$Consistency identity preserving the material $Z/A$ factor.

Important distinction: composition $Z_{\rm eff}$ is a target-material bookkeeping quantity; projectile $z_{\rm eff}(E)$ in §3.5 is a different physical concept describing charge-state reduction of a slow heavy ion.

9 · CSDA range

EquationUse
$$\boxed{R_{\rm CSDA}(E_0)=\int_0^{E_0}\frac{dE}{S_{\rm total}(E)}}$$Continuous-slowing-down approximation range in g/cm².
$$S(E)=-\frac1\rho\frac{dE}{dx}$$Mass stopping power appearing in the range integral.
$$x_{\rm physical}=\frac{\Delta x_{\rm mass}}{\rho}$$Convert areal density (g/cm²) to physical thickness (cm).

The application reads the range from the supplied tabulated data rather than numerically integrating the analytic stopping formula. The equation above is the physical definition represented by the table.

10 · Log–log interpolation

EquationUse
$$\ln S(E)=\ln S_1+\frac{\ln E-\ln E_1}{\ln E_2-\ln E_1}\left(\ln S_2-\ln S_1\right)$$Interpolate an arbitrary energy between two NIST points.
$$S(E)=\exp\!\big(\ln S(E)\big)$$Recover the physical stopping-power value.
$$S\propto E^n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ln S=n\ln E+\mathrm{const.}$$Reason log–log interpolation is locally natural for power-law-like data.

The code explicitly refuses extrapolation outside the tabulated energy range.

11 · Bragg-curve depth–dose construction

EquationUse
$$R(x)=R_{\rm CSDA}(E_0)-x$$Residual areal range after traveling depth $x$.
$$R(E(x))=R(x)$$Residual energy is obtained by inverting the tabulated range curve.
$$D(x)\propto S_{\rm total}(E(x))$$Idealized relative dose proxy.
$$D_{\rm rel}(x)=100\,\frac{S_{\rm total}(E(x))}{\max_xS_{\rm total}(E(x))}$$Normalized dose plotted by the Bragg Peak tab.
$$D(x_{R_p})/D_{\max}=p/100,\qquad p=90,80,50$$Definition used to identify distal R90/R80/R50 landmarks.

The depth grid is concentrated near the end of range by sampling residual range logarithmically. The final segment below the minimum tabulated energy is a phenomenological linear taper to $E=S=0$ for plotting only.

12 · Beam attenuation through multiple layers

Equation / operationUse in code
$$\Delta x_{\rm mass}=\rho\,\Delta x_{\rm cm}$$Convert physical layer thickness to g/cm².
$$\Delta x_{\rm mass}=\rho\,\frac{\Delta x_{\rm mm}}{10}$$Convert mm thickness to g/cm².
$$R_{\rm in}=R(E_{\rm in})$$Read incoming residual range from the tabulated curve.
$$R_{\rm out}=R_{\rm in}-\Delta x_{\rm mass}$$Subtract the layer's mass thickness.
$$E_{\rm out}=R^{-1}(R_{\rm out})$$Invert the same tabulated range curve to obtain exit energy.
$$R_{\rm out}\le0\quad\Rightarrow\quad E_{\rm out}=0$$Beam is fully stopped in that layer.
$$S(z)=S(E(z))$$Stopping power along the layer depth curve.

This is deliberately a range-subtraction method, not a thin-layer approximation $S(E)\Delta x$. It therefore remains consistent with the tabulated CSDA range data.

13 · Universal Model: low-energy branch + corrected Bethe–Bloch branch

The current Universal Model in the file is a blended heavy-particle model. The global material dependence is carried by $C_m$ and $E_t$, the crossover is controlled by $F$, and an optional localized asymmetric peak/dip factor is applied after blending.

EquationRole
$$C_m=2.28102253\times10^5\,M^{-0.09008080}I^{-0.70953564}(Z/A)^{0.62120103}$$Global material/projectile scaling for the low-energy coefficient.
$$E_t=2.74829614\times10^{-6}\,M^{1.57798691}I^{0.24764330}(Z/A)^{0.48478493}$$Global crossover-energy scaling.
$$S_{\rm low}(E)=C_m\sqrt{E}\,G(\xi)$$Low-energy branch used by the current implementation.
$$\xi=\frac{E}{E_t}$$Dimensionless crossover variable.
$$G(\xi)=\exp\!\left[a\frac{\sqrt{\xi}}{1+\sqrt{\xi}}\right]$$Smooth shape modification of the low-energy branch.
$$a=1.18645614$$Global low-energy shape coefficient in the current global model.
$$F(\xi)=1-\exp(-\xi^q),\qquad q=1.68961473$$Monotonic blending function.
$$S_{\rm base}(E)=[1-F(\xi)]S_{\rm low}(E)+F(\xi)S_{\rm BB}(E)$$Blend low-energy and corrected Bethe–Bloch branches.
$$E_p=\lambda_pE_t$$Peak/dip location relative to the crossover scale.
$$P(E)=\exp\!\left[-\frac{\ln^2(E/E_p)}{2\sigma^2}\right]$$Localized log-energy peak/dip profile.
$$S_{\rm Universal}(E)=S_{\rm base}(E)\,[1+A_pP(E)]$$Final Universal Model value scored against NIST.
$$\sigma=\begin{cases}\sigma_L,&E\lt E_p\\\sigma_R,&E\ge E_p\end{cases}$$Asymmetric left/right peak width.

Current global peak defaults

ParameterCurrent valueMeaning
$A_p$$-0.71065436$Peak amplitude; negative means a localized dip relative to the base model.
$\lambda_p$$1.05692429$Peak position in units of $E_t$.
$\sigma_L$$1.50633478$Low-energy-side log-width.
$\sigma_R$$0.64293593$High-energy-side log-width.

Per-material mode: the code can refit $C_m,E_t,q,a,A_p,\lambda_p,\sigma_L,\sigma_R$ for one material. The material-specific fit is performed by a dependency-free Nelder–Mead minimizer on the mean squared relative residual.

EquationPer-material fit
$$r_i=\frac{S_{\rm model}(E_i)-S_{\rm NIST}(E_i)}{S_{\rm NIST}(E_i)}$$Relative residual.
$$J=\frac1N\sum_i r_i^2$$Objective minimized by the per-material Universal Model fit.
$$C_m=e^{x_0},\quad E_t=e^{x_1},\quad q=e^{x_2},\quad \lambda_p=e^{x_5},\quad \sigma_{L,R}=\max(0.02,e^{x_{6,7}})$$Positive-parameter transforms used internally by the optimizer.

14 · Reduced low-energy models

The Reduced Models tab tests progressively richer low-energy laws while keeping the same fixed corrected Bethe–Bloch high-energy branch and the same blending function.

ModelEquationFree parameters
Model 1$$S_{\rm low}^{(1)}=C\sqrt E$$$C$
Model 2$$S_{\rm low}^{(2)}=C\sqrt E\,\exp\!\left[\frac1{1+E/E_t}\right]$$$C,E_t$
Model 3$$S_{\rm low}^{(3)}=CE^n\exp\!\left[\frac{a}{1+E/E_t}\right]$$$C,E_t,a,n$
All$$S^{(k)}=[1-F(\xi)]S_{\rm low}^{(k)}+F(\xi)S_{\rm BB}$$Shared $q=1.68961473$

Global scaling laws used by the Reduced Models fit

EquationMeaning
$$C=C_0\left(\frac{M}{M_p}\right)^{c_M}\left(\frac{I}{100\,{\rm eV}}\right)^{c_I}\left(\frac{Z/A}{0.5}\right)^{c_Z}$$Global power-law scaling of $C$.
$$E_t=E_0\left(\frac{M}{M_p}\right)^{t_M}\left(\frac{I}{100\,{\rm eV}}\right)^{t_I}\left(\frac{Z/A}{0.5}\right)^{t_Z}$$Global power-law scaling of $E_t$.
$$a=a_0+a_M\ln(M/M_p)+a_I\ln(I/100\,{\rm eV})+a_Z\ln[(Z/A)/0.5]$$Global linear-log scaling of $a$.
$$n=n_0$$Global exponent in Model 3.

15 · Corrected Bethe–Bloch $Z_{\rm eff}$ inversion

The Search tab does not redefine the physical stopping formula. It holds $I_{\rm eff}$ and $A_{\rm eff}$ fixed and solves for a data-driven $Z_{\rm eff}$ such that the corrected-BB model equals the NIST value at each energy.

Equation / conditionUse
$$\frac{Z_{\rm eff}}{A_{\rm eff}}\equiv Z/A\quad\text{inside the CBB inversion}$$Pass the trial composition ratio into the stopping formula.
$$f(Z_{\rm eff})=S_{\rm CBB}(E;Z_{\rm eff},A_{\rm eff})-S_{\rm NIST}(E)$$Root function.
$$f(Z_{\rm eff})=0$$Definition of the fitted $Z_{\rm eff}$ at one energy.
$$Z_{\rm eff}\in[0.05,130]$$Search bracket used by the bisection solver.
$$Z_{\rm eff}^{\rm median}=\operatorname{median}\{Z_{\rm eff}(E_i)\}$$Per-material summary statistic.
$$\bar Z_{\rm eff}=\frac1N\sum_iZ_{\rm eff}(E_i)$$Per-material mean fitted value.
$$\sigma_Z=\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_i(Z_i-\bar Z)^2}$$Spread reported for the fitted values.

16 · Error metrics and statistical model-comparison equations

EquationDisplayed quantity
$$e_i=100\,\frac{S_i-S_{\rm NIST}}{S_{\rm NIST}}$$Signed percent difference.
$$r_i=\frac{S_i}{S_{\rm NIST}}=1+\frac{e_i}{100}$$Theory/NIST ratio.
$$\mathrm{MAPE}=\frac1N\sum_i|e_i|$$Mean absolute percent error.
$$\mathrm{RMS\%}=\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_ie_i^2}$$Root-mean-square percent difference.
$$\mathrm{Max|diff|\%}=\max_i|e_i|$$Maximum absolute percent difference.
$$\bar r=\frac1N\sum_ir_i$$Mean multiplicative ratio.
$$\chi^2=\sum_i\left(\frac{e_i/100}{0.05}\right)^2$$Common 5% relative model-discrepancy diagnostic.
$$\chi^2_{\rm red}=\frac{\chi^2}{N-k}$$Reduced chi-square; $k$ is the number of fitted parameters.
$$\mathrm{AIC}=N\ln\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}N\right)+2k$$AIC used for reduced-model comparison.
$$\mathrm{BIC}=N\ln\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}N\right)+k\ln N$$BIC used to select the preferred reduced model.
$$\mathrm{Winner}(m)=\arg\min_j\mathrm{MAPE}_{m,j}$$Material-level winner in the electron global analysis.
$$\mathrm{Global\ winner}=\arg\min_j\mathrm{MAPE}_{\rm pooled,j}$$Point-pooled global winner.

Statistical convention: the 5% scale is a model-discrepancy reference used consistently by this application; it is not a claim that every NIST tabulated point has an independent 5% experimental uncertainty.

17 · Proton/alpha same-velocity scaling

EquationUse
$$E_\alpha=\frac{M_\alpha}{M_p}E_p$$Nonrelativistic same-velocity energy scaling.
$$S_\alpha(E_\alpha)\approx z_\alpha^2S_p(E_p)$$Leading $z^2$ electronic stopping scaling at the same velocity.

At low velocity this simple relation breaks down because alpha effective-charge reduction and correction terms become important. This is why ASTAR is retained as an independent reference table.

Limitations and implementation boundaries

  • The supplied NIST ESTAR/PSTAR/ASTAR tables remain the reference data. The analytic formulas in this tab are transparent comparison models, not a byte-for-byte reconstruction of every NIST procedure.
  • The compact density effect is an asymptotic approximation. The Electron tab additionally provides a universal Sternheimer–Peierls bridge, but it does not have NIST's full material-specific Sternheimer coefficient set.
  • The shell parameterization is explicitly switched off below $\beta\gamma=0.1$ rather than extrapolated.
  • ESTAR radiative stopping is not analytically reconstructed in the application.
  • Nuclear stopping is represented through the supplied PSTAR/ASTAR reference values rather than an in-browser first-principles ZBL cross-section integration.
  • The Bragg and multilayer calculations are CSDA constructions and do not model range straggling, multiple Coulomb scattering, nuclear-interaction tails, or detailed transport.
  • The Universal Model's global coefficients are empirical/global-fit coefficients. Its low-energy law should therefore be interpreted as a phenomenological model constrained by the supplied NIST systems.
  • The 5% chi-square scale is a model-discrepancy convention used by this application and should not be interpreted as an experimental uncertainty for each tabulated datum.

Quick start

  1. Pick a particle database — ESTAR (electrons), PSTAR (protons), or ASTAR (helium ions) — from the sidebar dropdown or by clicking its icon in the sidebar navigation.
  2. Type into Material search to filter the material list (try "water", "bone", "muscle", or an element name), then choose one from the Material dropdown.
  3. Enter an Energy in MeV.
  4. Click Calculate — the results table, plot, and material panel all update together.

The database loads fully offline on first launch; the status line at the bottom of the sidebar confirms when it's ready ("Database loaded · fully offline").

The tab bar at the top switches between six views: Calculator (single-energy lookup, described in this section), Comparison (simplified formula vs. NIST across the whole grid — §man-comparison), Search (data-driven Zeff fitting — §man-search), Bragg Peak (depth–dose curve for a mono-energetic beam — §man-bragg), Theory (the physics reference), and this Manual.

Particle database & material

The three particle databases behave slightly differently downstream — for example only PSTAR/ASTAR split stopping power into electronic and nuclear components, and only ESTAR splits into collision and radiative components (see Theory → §1). Switching particles automatically repopulates the material list from that database's material set and refreshes the crumb label in the top bar.

The material list holds 277 materials spanning single elements and NIST-standard compounds/mixtures (biological tissues, detector materials, shielding materials, etc.). The search box filters this list by name as you type — clear it to see the full list again.

Energy input & Calculate

Energy is always entered in MeV. The app performs log–log interpolation between the nearest tabulated grid points (Theory → §10) — it does not extrapolate. If your energy falls outside the material's tabulated range, the status banner turns neutral (not green) and reports the valid range, e.g. "Energy outside tabulated range: 0.001–10000 MeV"; the results table will show — for any quantity it cannot evaluate.

Press Calculate (or just edit the Energy field — it recalculates automatically on input) to refresh everything downstream: the results table, the diagnostic theory comparison, the plot's marked point, and the material properties panel.

Reading the results

The Interpolated result card lists every quantity the selected database provides at your chosen energy, each with its unit. Depending on the particle, this includes some subset of:

QuantityApplies toMeaning
Collision stopping powerESTAREnergy loss to atomic excitation/ionization (mass stopping power)
Radiative stopping powerESTAREnergy loss to bremsstrahlung
Total stopping powerallSum of the applicable components
Electronic stopping powerPSTAR, ASTAREnergy loss to atomic electrons (Bethe–Bloch)
Nuclear stopping powerPSTAR, ASTAREnergy loss to elastic nuclear recoil
CSDA rangeallContinuous-slowing-down-approximation path length (Theory → §8)

Below the table, a small diagnostic panel compares NIST's tabulated electronic stopping power against a simplified Bethe–Bloch calculation this app computes itself (PSTAR/ASTAR only — disabled for ESTAR, since electrons use a different formula, see below).

For a fuller comparison across the whole energy grid — including electrons — switch to the Comparison tab (§man-comparison). It runs the simplified Bethe formula for protons/alphas or the Møller/Berger–Seltzer formula for electrons (Theory → §2, §4) at every tabulated energy, plots both curves together, and lists a scrollable energy-by-energy comparison table. For ESTAR it compares against collision stopping power only — the Møller formula has no bremsstrahlung term, so it cannot be checked against ESTAR's radiative or total columns.

Both diagnostics are meant to give a feel for how much the shell, density-effect, Barkas, and Bloch corrections shift the result away from the textbook formula — neither is a replacement for the NIST value.

Two extra derived statistics are computed for convenience: the radiative fraction (ESTAR) or electronic/nuclear fractions (PSTAR/ASTAR), and Total dE/dx in MeV/cm, obtained by multiplying the total mass stopping power by the material's density.

The plot

The chart shows the full tabulated curve for the selected quantity (chosen from the dropdown at the top-right of the chart header) across the entire energy grid, with your current energy/value marked as a highlighted point. Controls above the chart:

  • Axis scale — log–log (default, best for viewing the full range), log–linear, or linear–linear.
  • Color palette, symbol palette, line style — purely cosmetic, useful when comparing screenshots across materials or exporting a figure.
  • Quantity selector — switches which tabulated column is plotted (e.g. total vs. electronic vs. nuclear stopping power, or CSDA range).

The plot is fully interactive (pan, zoom, hover for exact values) via Plotly — scroll to zoom, drag to pan, and double-click to reset the view.

Exporting data

Two independent export paths are available:

  • Full-curve export — the .dat / .txt / .json buttons in the chart header download the entire tabulated curve for the current particle/material (every energy point NIST provides, not just your interpolated value).
  • Export CSV — the sidebar's Export CSV button produces the same full curve in comma-separated form, labeled with particle, material ID, and material name on every row.

None of these exports apply your interpolation — they are the raw NIST grid, so you can re-interpolate or re-analyze independently of this app.

Material properties panel

The right-hand card summarizes the selected material: density, mean excitation energy $I$, the stopping-power $Z/A$, derived electron density, elemental composition, composition-average $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and — once you've calculated — the current particle's derived statistics at your energy. The composition rows show both the supplied mass fraction $w_i$ and the derived atomic fraction $f_i$.

For compounds and mixtures, the displayed $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ are calculated from the atomic fractions described in Theory → §7a. Their ratio is exactly the material's $Z/A$, so these two displayed values provide a compact composition summary without changing the NIST stopping-power calculation.

7a · Understanding $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$

For an elemental material, $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}=Z$ and $A_{\mathrm{eff}}=A$. For a compound or mixture, the app first converts mass fractions to atomic fractions:

$$f_i=\frac{w_i/A_i}{\sum_j w_j/A_j}.$$

It then calculates

$$A_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{1}{\sum_i w_i/A_i},\qquad Z_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{\sum_i w_iZ_i/A_i}{\sum_i w_i/A_i}.$$

The key consistency relation is

$$\frac{Z_{\mathrm{eff}}}{A_{\mathrm{eff}}}=\sum_iw_i\frac{Z_i}{A_i}=\left(\frac ZA\right)_{\!\text{material}}.$$

Do not interpret this $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ as a universal effective atomic number. Different radiation processes use different effective-Z definitions. In this stopping-power application, $Z/A$ and electron density are the fundamental composition quantities.

Comparison tab

This tab checks the app's own simplified stopping-power formulas against the full NIST tables, across the entire tabulated energy grid at once (rather than just your one Calculator energy).

  1. Pick a Particle and use Material search to filter, then choose a Material — the same 277-material list as the Calculator tab.
  2. Click Calculate & plot.

The chart overlays the theory curve (Bethe–Bloch for protons/alphas, Møller/Berger–Seltzer for electrons — Theory → §2, §4) against NIST's tabulated points, shown as filled points with no connecting line. Axis scale, color, symbol and line style controls above the chart work the same way as on the Calculator tab.

Below the chart, a summary row reports the RMS percent difference over all valid points, and a scrollable table lists every tabulated energy with the theory value, the NIST value, their ratio, absolute difference, and percent difference. For ESTAR, the comparison is against the collision stopping power column only — the theory formula used here has no radiative term (Theory → §5), so it cannot be checked against ESTAR's radiative or total columns.

Disagreement grows at low energy: the theory formulas implemented here omit the density effect, shell correction, and Barkas/Bloch corrections (Theory → §3), all of which matter most as the particle slows down. Use this tab to see exactly how much those omitted corrections are worth for a given material, not as a substitute for the NIST value.

The .dat / .txt / .json buttons in the chart header export the full comparison table (energy, theory value, NIST value, ratio, differences) for the current particle/material.

How to read proton and alpha curves

For protons and alphas, several cumulative theory curves are drawn. Start with Bethe–Bloch (uncorrected). Each following curve adds one more correction in sequence: Density effect → Shell → Barkas → Bloch → Effective charge. This makes the physical contribution of each correction visible across energy.

  • NIST data always remains the fixed reference: filled red circles with no connecting line. Its color and symbol are not changed by the comparison controls.
  • Color, symbol and line-style controls apply to the main theory presentation, while cumulative correction layers use clearly separated line colors and dash patterns so proton and alpha curves remain visible on the same background.
  • Legend interaction: click a correction name to hide or restore that layer. This is useful when two curves are physically close.
  • Low energy: effective charge and shell effects can strongly change heavy-particle stopping power, so inspect the left side of the log-energy plot carefully.

For electrons, the comparison uses the electron (Møller/Berger–Seltzer) theory branch, and the NIST reference remains the same fixed red-circle dataset. Cumulative correction layers are drawn here too — Density effect → Shell → Barkas → Bloch — reusing the same Shell, Barkas and Bloch checkboxes as protons/alphas, but evaluated at electron kinematics (Theory → §4). Only the Effective charge checkbox has no effect for electrons, since it models a heavy ion's bound-electron pickup at low velocity, which a bare lepton has no analogue of.

Search tab

This tab fits a data-driven, corrected Bethe–Bloch (CBB) $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ against NIST: I_eff and A_eff are held fixed at their database/composition values, and $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is solved by bisection so corrected-BB($Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$) reproduces the NIST value. It reuses the Particle, Material, and correction-layer selections currently set on the Comparison tab (§man-comparison) — change those there first.

  1. Check Fit Zeff to NIST at each energy to solve $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ point-by-point for the material currently selected on the Comparison tab, plotted against the nominal (composition) $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  2. Click Calculate Zeff — all materials to run the same per-energy fit across every material in the PSTAR and ASTAR databases at once and summarize each as a median/mean fitted $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$.

A point marked "—" means no $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ in [0.05, 130] reproduces the NIST value at that energy for the currently selected correction layers. A roughly flat fitted $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(E)$ close to the nominal composition value means the standard corrections already explain the material dependence; a systematic trend or offset is the signal a $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$-based correction term would need to capture. Proton/alpha only — electrons are not supported by this fit.

The .dat / .txt / .json buttons export the per-energy fit for the current material; the .csv / .json buttons on the all-materials panel export the full per-material summary table.

Bragg Peak tab

This tab turns a single-energy beam into a depth–dose (Bragg) curve — how relative dose varies with depth as the beam slows down and stops. The physics behind it is in Theory → §12.

  1. Pick a Particle (defaults to PSTAR — protons — since electrons don't show a true Bragg peak).
  2. Use Material search and the Material dropdown to pick the absorbing medium.
  3. Enter the Initial energy in MeV — this is the beam energy at the surface, before any slowing down.
  4. Click Calculate Bragg curve.

The chart plots relative dose (0–100%, normalized to the peak) against depth. Controls above the chart:

  • Axis scale — log–log, log–linear, linear–log, or lin–lin (default) for the depth/dose axes.
  • Depth unit — cm, mm, or g/cm² (areal density, independent of the material's physical density).

The legend marks the Bragg peak itself and the R90/R80/R50 landmarks (Theory → §12). Below the chart, a table lists each landmark's depth, residual range, residual energy, and relative dose. The .dat / .txt / .json buttons export the full depth–dose curve, log-spaced in residual range as described in the Theory tab.

Remember this is an idealized CSDA curve: no range straggling, no multiple Coulomb scattering, and no nuclear-interaction buildup/falloff, so the peak is sharper and taller than a real measured Bragg curve (Theory → §12).

Tips & troubleshooting

  • The theme toggle (sun/moon icon, top right) switches between light and dark and is remembered across visits via localStorage.
  • If a value shows as —, either the energy is outside the tabulated range for that material, or that quantity doesn't apply to the current particle (e.g. radiative stopping power for PSTAR).
  • Everything runs fully offline from the bundled dataset — no network requests are made once the page has loaded, so results are reproducible without an internet connection.
  • For a comparison across particles at "the same" physical situation, remember the proton/alpha scaling relation in Theory → §9 rather than expecting ESTAR, PSTAR and ASTAR curves to line up directly — they describe different projectiles.
  • The Calculator, Comparison and Bragg Peak tabs each keep their own independent particle/material selection — changing the material on one tab does not change the others, so double-check you're looking at the material you expect on each tab. The Search tab has no selection of its own; it reuses whatever particle/material/correction layers are currently set on the Comparison tab.

How the Comparison Plot Is Ordered

The Comparison plot builds the stopping-power model cumulatively. Each new curve contains the previous model plus one additional correction.

CurveMeaning
Bethe–BlochBase model
BB + Density effectBethe–Bloch with the density correction included
+ Shell correctionBB + Density + Shell
+ Barkas correctionBB + Density + Shell + Barkas
+ Bloch correctionBB + Density + Shell + Barkas + Bloch
+ Effective chargeFinal corrected model, especially important for protons and alpha particles at low energy
NISTReference data shown separately
$$ \boxed{ \text{BB} \;\rightarrow\; \text{BB + Density} \;\rightarrow\; +\text{Shell} \;\rightarrow\; +\text{Barkas} \;\rightarrow\; +\text{Bloch} \;\rightarrow\; +\text{Effective Charge} \;\rightarrow\; \text{NIST} } $$

Important: “BB + Density” is not the density correction by itself. It is the original Bethe–Bloch model after the density correction has been added. Every following curve is cumulative.

Sources

References

The primary sources behind the data and the physics models implemented in this app. Each entry links to the original document. Grouped by what they underpin — the underlying data, the corrected Bethe–Bloch model, the shell/Barkas/Bloch/effective-charge corrections, the density effect, the Møller/Berger–Seltzer electron branch, and the low-energy branch used by the Universal Model.

NIST ESTAR / PSTAR / ASTAR — the tabulated data

ReferenceRelevance
NIST ESTAR, PSTAR, ASTAR — Introduction ↗ Official NIST documentation for the stopping-power/range databases this app's ESTAR/PSTAR/ASTAR tables are drawn from; describes the ICRU-based methods and the standard energy grids reproduced here.
NIST Standard Reference Database 124 (SRD 124) ↗ The current NIST landing page for the database, including the 2017 update and the ICRU Report 90 re-evaluation summary for graphite, air and water.
Berger, M.J. (1992). ESTAR, PSTAR and ASTAR: Computer Programs for Calculating Stopping-Power and Range Tables for Electrons, Protons, and Helium Ions. NISTIR 4999 ↗ The original technical report describing the ESTAR/PSTAR/ASTAR codes and the ICRU 37 / ICRU 49 methods they implement.
NIST ESTAR/PSTAR/ASTAR — full reference list ↗ NIST's own bibliography for the database: Bethe (1930, 1932), Bloch (1933), Bichsel (1990, 1991), ICRU Reports 37 and 49, and the other papers the tabulated values ultimately rest on.

Corrected Bethe–Bloch model (protons & alphas, Theory §2)

ReferenceRelevance
Bethe (1930, 1932); Bloch (1933) — via NIST reference list ↗ The original Born-approximation stopping-power derivation and its extension, forming the uncorrected Bethe–Bloch backbone $S_{\rm BB}=K\frac{Z}{A}\frac{z^2}{\beta^2}L_0$ used in this app's Comparison, Universal Model and Reduced Model tabs.
Particle Data Group — Review of Particle Physics ↗ Standard modern reference for the full corrected Bethe–Bloch formula (density-effect, shell and high-order terms) in the notation this app follows for $S_{\rm BB}$, $\delta(X)$ and the stopping-number expansion.

Shell, Barkas, Bloch and effective-charge corrections (Theory §2–§3)

ReferenceRelevance
Barkas, W.H., Berger, M.J. (1964). Tables of Energy Losses and Ranges of Heavy Charged Particles. NAS–NRC Publication 1133 / NASA SP-3013 — via NIST reference list ↗ The classical source of the low-velocity shell correction $C/Z$ this app applies to the proton/alpha Bethe–Bloch branch; NIST's own PSTAR/ASTAR shell-correction values trace back to this compilation.
Ashley, J.C., Ritchie, R.H., Brandt, W. (1972). Z³ effect in the stopping power of matter for charged particles. Phys. Rev. B5, 2393 — via NIST reference list ↗ The theoretical account of the odd-in-$z$ (Barkas) correction this app switches on with the Barkas checkbox; explains why protons and antiprotons of equal speed lose energy at slightly different rates.
Bichsel, H. (1990). Barkas effect and effective charge in the theory of stopping power. Phys. Rev. A41, 3642 — via NIST reference list ↗ Ties the Barkas ($z^3$) term to the low-velocity effective-charge reduction of heavy ions (electron pickup at low $\beta$); the basis for this app's combined Barkas / effective-charge treatment in the proton and alpha branches.
Bloch, F. (1933). Zur Bremsung rasch bewegter Teilchen beim Durchgang durch Materie. Ann. d. Physik 16, 285 — via NIST reference list ↗ The original $z^4$ (Bloch) correction bridging the classical Bohr and quantum Born stopping-power limits, applied here as the Bloch checkbox on top of the shell and Barkas terms.

This app's Effective charge checkbox implements the low-velocity charge-reduction of protons and alphas motivated by the Barkas/Bichsel treatment above; it has no analogue for electrons (Theory §4), since a bare lepton has no bound-electron population to pick up or lose.

Density-effect correction δ (Theory §2.1, Electron tab Sternheimer–Peierls bridge)

ReferenceRelevance
Sternheimer, R.M., Berger, M.J., Seltzer, S.M. (1984). Density effect for the ionization loss of charged particles in various substances. Atomic Data and Nuclear Data Tables 30, 261 ↗ The per-material Sternheimer coefficients ($C$, $a$, $m$, $X_0$, $X_1$) that NIST uses for precision δ; this app's "compact" density-effect asymptote and its universal (non-tabulated) $X_0,X_1,m$ rules are simplified stand-ins for this table — see Theory §2.1.
Sternheimer, R.M., Peierls, R.F. (1971). General expression for the density effect for the ionization loss of charged particles. Phys. Rev. B3, 3681 — cited here ↗ The original three-branch $\delta(X)$ construction (low-$X$, bridge, high-$X$ asymptote) that the Electron tab's "Sternheimer–Peierls" density-effect curve reconstructs without a per-material table.

Electron collision stopping power — Møller / Berger–Seltzer branch (Theory §4)

ReferenceRelevance
NIST ESTAR — Introduction ↗ Documents that ESTAR's electron collision stopping power follows the Møller cross section (with density-effect correction), the formula this app's Electron tab reproduces separately from the heavy-particle Bethe–Bloch branch — see the "important implementation distinction" note in Theory §1.
ICRU Report 37 (1984), Stopping Powers for Electrons and Positrons — via NIST reference list ↗ The ICRU report whose electron stopping-power methodology (including the Møller/Berger–Seltzer collision term) ESTAR reproduces by default; the authoritative source for the electron-specific formula used here.
Berger, M.J., Seltzer, S.M. (1982). Stopping Powers and Ranges of Electrons and Positrons. NBSIR 82-2550 ↗ The direct source of the Møller collision cross section as tabulated by Berger and Seltzer — the specific "Møller / Berger–Seltzer branch" this app's Electron tab evaluates and compares against ESTAR, built on Møller's original 1931 relativistic electron–electron scattering theory.

Low-energy branch and Lindhard–Scharff scaling (Universal Model, Theory §13)

ReferenceRelevance
Mangiarotti, A. et al. A survey of energy loss calculations for heavy ions between 1 and 100 keV ↗ An accessible survey covering the Lindhard–Scharff(–Schiøtt) low-velocity electronic-stopping theory ($S_e\propto\sqrt E$) that motivates this app's $C_m\sqrt E$ low-energy branch and its blend into the Bethe–Bloch branch via $F(\xi)$ — see Universal Model tab and Theory §13.

The specific global scaling laws $C_m,E_t\propto I^{a}(Z/A)^{b}$, the blending function $F(\xi)$, and the peak-correction factor $P(E)$ are this app's own empirical fits to the 148 embedded PSTAR/ASTAR systems (Universal Model tab) — they are not themselves published results, only motivated by the Lindhard–Scharff regime above.

This app is an independent, offline implementation built from the sources above; it is not affiliated with or endorsed by NIST or the ICRU. The bundled ESTAR/PSTAR/ASTAR tables remain the reference data throughout — every analytic model in the Comparison, Universal Model, Reduced Models and Electron tabs is scored against them, never the other way around.
